tagline: An Adirondack road links mountain country with Roosevelt’s journey to the presidency.
intro: The Roosevelt-Marcy Trail follows 40 miles of Route 28N between Long Lake and North Creek through the central Adirondacks. Mountain slopes, lakes and the Hudson River shape the drive, with two lanes passing through Newcomb. It entered New York’s Scenic Byway Program in 1992; the state transportation department identifies scenic, recreational, historic and natural themes. Route 28N itself extends farther west to Blue Mountain Lake; the scenic corridor covers the portion beyond its overlap with Route 30.

The road began as a highway from Warren County to Long Lake, carrying traffic for Newcomb’s iron industry and Minerva’s lumber trade. In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt traveled overnight toward North Creek after learning that President William McKinley was near death. At the station, he learned he would become president. New York took control of the road in 1909, and the Route 28N number followed in 1930. The Roosevelt-Marcy Memorial Highway name arrived in the early 1980s.

Start at Long Lake, where 28N separates from Route 30 and heads east toward Newcomb, passing south of Rich Lake. Beyond Harris Lake, the road turns southeast into Winebrook Hills, then south through Aiden Lair and Minerva. Past Moxham Mountain, it crosses the Hudson and ends at Route 28 in North Creek.

moments.title: Goodnow Mountain
moments.text: A 60-foot steel fire tower stands on Goodnow Mountain, a 2,664-foot Adirondack summit. Landowners and lumbermen helped secure the tower after the mountain was chosen for a fire observation station in 1921. Fire watching ended after the 1979 season, and the tower later passed to SUNY College of Forestry. The college restored both tower and cabin. The mountain’s name recalls Sylvester Goodnow, who settled at its base in the 1820s; the later Huntington owners donated their property to the university in 1932.

moments.title: Santanoni Preserve
moments.text: Camp Santanoni’s main lodge joined six separate buildings beneath a shared roof and porch system. Banker Robert C. Pruyn commissioned architect Robert H. Robertson to design his summer residence, and the Main Camp buildings went up in 1892–93. Builders used 1,500 spruce trees in the log construction, with birch bark on walls and fieldstone fireplaces inside. The estate later became state property. Restoration by the state, Adirondack Architectural Heritage and the Town of Newcomb began in 1993. The Main Camp sits on Newcomb Lake, 4.7 miles from the Gate Lodge complex.

moments.title: North Creek
moments.text: North Creek’s station has vertical board siding and a broad, overhanging roof supported by struts. The original station opened in 1871 as the Adirondack Railway’s northern terminus; the station building described here dates to 1874. Trains served garnet mining and tanning, and the line did not extend beyond North Creek until freight service reached Tahawus in 1944. This is where Roosevelt learned of his accession to the presidency after McKinley’s death. Ski trains brought another kind of traveler from 1934 until the outbreak of World War II. Part of the complex now houses the North Creek Depot Museum.
